stages.title: Characteristics of life
stages.hook: A candle flame grows, moves and uses up fuel. Is it alive? What would you need to check?
explain: Scientists say living things share seven features: movement, respiration (getting energy from food), sensitivity (reacting to the surroundings), growth, reproduction (making young), excretion (getting rid of waste) and nutrition (taking in food). A short way to remember them is MRS GREN.
A flame seems to grow and use fuel, but it does not reproduce, sense or make waste in the way a living thing does. So it is not alive.
Not every living thing shows every feature at every moment. A seed is not growing while it is dry, but it is alive and can grow when it gets water.

example.q: A mushroom grows, makes spores and takes in food from rotting wood. Is it alive?
steps: Growth: yes, it gets bigger.
Reproduction: yes, spores make new mushrooms.
Nutrition: yes, it takes in food.
It meets the tests, so it is alive.

analogies.home: A cat reacts to a noise, eats, grows and has kittens. A toy cat does none of these.
analogies.farm: Crops grow, need water and make seeds. A tractor moves but does not grow or reproduce.
analogies.tech: A robot can move and sense, but it does not grow, eat or reproduce on its own.

stages.mnemonic: MRS GREN: Movement, Respiration, Sensitivity, Growth, Reproduction, Excretion, Nutrition.
terms: Releasing energy from food inside cells.
Removing waste made by the body.
Detecting and reacting to changes around you.
Making new living things of the same kind.

misc.right: Rivers, clouds and cars move, but they do not meet all the features of life. Living things show all seven.

stages.limits: Viruses are a borderline case. They reproduce only inside living cells, so scientists still debate whether to call them alive.

trip.prompt: Find the list of features scientists use to define life. Which ones can you spot in a plant?

questions.q: What does the R in MRS GREN stand for twice?
questions.why: R is for respiration and for reproduction.

questions.q: What is excretion?
questions.why: Excretion removes waste products made by the body.

questions.q: A Venus flytrap closes when an insect touches it. Which feature is this?
questions.why: Reacting to a touch is sensitivity.

questions.q: A car moves, uses fuel and gives out exhaust. Why is it still not alive?
o: It cannot grow or reproduce by itself
It is much too big and heavy to count
It is made of metal and plastic only
questions.why: Living things must show all seven features. A car does not grow, sense or reproduce.

questions.q: Dry bean seeds do not grow in a packet but come alive in wet soil. What does this show?
o: A living thing may wait until conditions are right
Seeds are never alive until planted in soil
Wet soil turns dead seeds into living ones
Water itself is a living thing
questions.why: Seeds are alive but resting until they get water and warmth.

questions.q: Match each feature to an example.
questions.why: Each example shows one feature of life.

questions.q: Why is a flame not classed as a living thing even though it moves and uses fuel?
questions.model: A flame cannot reproduce, grow from inside or sense its surroundings like a living thing. It shows only a few features, not all seven.
questions.why: Life needs all of the features, not just movement and using fuel.

questions.q: Which is a sign of respiration in a mouse?
o: It uses food and oxygen to release energy
It grows a thicker coat of fur to keep warm
It sleeps for most of the day
It has whiskers that sense touch
questions.why: Respiration releases energy from food.

questions.q: Put in order the steps of an experiment to test if seeds are alive.
questions.why: A fair test goes from question to observation to conclusion.

questions.q: A scientist finds a new object that grows, reacts to light, takes in food and has offspring. What should she conclude?
o: It is probably a living thing
It is probably a kind of rock
It is probably a machine of some kind
It is probably a cloud of gas
questions.why: It shows the features of life.

panel.q: Which statement is best about a virus?
o: It is a borderline case because it reproduces only inside cells
It is clearly a plant that lost its leaves
It is clearly a non-living rock or grain of sand
It grows and feeds by itself in water
panel.why: Viruses lack many features of life, so scientists debate their status.

panel.q: A plant leans toward a window. Which two features are shown?
panel.why: It senses light and grows toward it.

panel.q: A student says a fire is alive because it eats wood, grows and gives off waste smoke. Explain a flaw in her thinking.
panel.model: A fire does not reproduce, is not made of cells and does not sense and respond. Living things must show all the features.
panel.why: A fire copies some features but lacks the others and is not made of cells.

teach.topic: How scientists decide if something is alive
teach.model: Scientists check a list of seven features: movement, respiration, sensitivity, growth, reproduction, excretion and nutrition. A living thing shows all of them. A candle flame shows only a few, so it is not alive.

points.ask: Can you name some of the features?
Can you give an example of something that is not alive?

stages.title: Cells and organisms
stages.hook: You are made of billions of tiny parts. Some living things are made of just one. How can one tiny part be a whole living thing?
explain: Cells are the tiny building blocks of living things. Most are too small to see without a microscope. An organism is a whole living thing.

Some organisms are made of one cell, like an amoeba. Others have many cells, like a tree or a person. In many-celled organisms, cells of the same kind form tissues, tissues form organs and organs work in systems.
Most animal cells have a nucleus (control centre), cytoplasm (where jobs happen) and a cell membrane (the skin of the cell). Plant cells also have a cell wall and chloroplasts.

example.q: Which is bigger: a tissue or an organ? Give an example.
steps: Cells make tissues, such as muscle tissue.
Different tissues combine to make an organ, such as the heart.
So an organ is bigger.
example.a: An organ, such as the heart, is made of tissues.

analogies.home: Bricks make a wall and walls make a house. Cells make tissues and tissues make organs.
analogies.city: A city has many buildings. A body has many cells working together.
analogies.music: One player is a cell. A whole orchestra of different players is like an organ system.

stages.mnemonic: Cell, tissue, organ, system, organism: Cats Take Our Sweet Oranges.
terms: The smallest unit of a living thing.
The control centre of a cell.
A group of similar cells doing the same job.

misc.wrong: All living things are made of many cells.
misc.right: Some organisms, such as bacteria and amoebas, are made of a single cell.

trip.prompt: Find a picture of an animal cell. Name two parts that you can label.

questions.q: What is the control centre of a cell?
questions.why: The nucleus controls the cell's activities.

questions.q: Which organism has just one cell?
questions.why: An amoeba is a single-celled organism.

questions.q: What do we need to see most cells?
questions.why: Cells are too small for the unaided eye.

questions.q: Put in order from smallest to largest.
questions.why: Cells form tissues, tissues form organs, organs form systems, systems form the organism.

questions.q: Match the cell part to its job.
pairs: Controls what goes in and out
questions.why: Each part has a role.

questions.q: Muscle cells together form which level of organisation?
questions.why: A group of similar cells is a tissue.

questions.q: Which part is found in plant cells but NOT animal cells?
questions.why: Only plant cells have a cell wall.

questions.q: The stomach is made of muscle, glandular and other tissues. What is the stomach?
questions.why: An organ is made of several tissues.

questions.q: Why does a large animal need many cells instead of just one giant cell?
questions.model: Many small cells can specialise in different jobs and work together as tissues and organs. A single huge cell would struggle to take in enough materials through its surface for its size.
questions.why: Specialised cells make a large body efficient.

questions.q: An amoeba must do every life process inside one cell. What does this tell you?
o: A single cell can carry out all life processes
It must grow as large as a mouse to work properly
It has no nucleus or other parts inside
It cannot be a living thing
questions.why: A single cell can be a complete organism.

panel.q: Why do leaves look green under a microscope?
o: They have only thick cell walls
They contain only water and salts
panel.why: Chloroplasts hold the green pigment chlorophyll.

panel.q: A student sees tiny cells in an onion skin. Why can they be seen separately?
o: Each cell has a wall and boundary
The cells have no boundary at all
The cells are huge and easy to spot
All the cells have the same bright colour
panel.why: Cell walls and membranes outline each cell.

panel.q: Which statement is correct?
o: Cells are the basic units of all organisms
Only animals are built from cells, not plants
panel.why: All organisms are made of cells.

teach.model: Cells are the tiny building blocks of living things. Some living things, like amoebas, are made of one cell. Others, like people, are made of billions. Similar cells form tissues, tissues form organs.

points.ask: Do all living things have the same number of cells?
How do cells make a body?

stages.title: Basic human anatomy
stages.hook: Your body works while you sleep. Who is running the show?
explain: The body has organ systems that each do a job. The skeleton supports us. Muscles move us. The heart and blood vessels form the circulatory system. Lungs help us breathe. The stomach and intestines digest food. The brain and nerves control the body.
These systems work together. When you run, muscles use energy from food, the lungs bring in oxygen, and the heart pumps blood to carry oxygen to the muscles.
An adult skeleton has 206 bones. Joints, such as the knee and elbow, let bones move. Muscles pull on bones with tendons.

example.q: Which systems help when you climb stairs?
steps: Muscles and bones move your legs.
Lungs take in more oxygen.
The heart pumps blood faster.
example.a: The muscular, skeletal, respiratory and circulatory systems.

analogies.home: A house has pipes, wiring and walls. The body has blood vessels, nerves and bones.
analogies.city: Roads move goods like blood moves oxygen.
analogies.sport: A football team works together like body systems.

stages.mnemonic: Bones hold, muscles pull, heart pumps, lungs fill, stomach grinds, brain thinks.
terms: The bones that support the body.
Tissue that pulls to make parts move.
Breaking food into tiny pieces the body can use.
The movement of blood around the body.

misc.right: Muscles can only pull. Pairs of muscles work in opposite ways to bend and straighten a joint.

trip.prompt: Find the list of organ systems. Pick one and say what it does.

questions.q: How many bones does an adult skeleton have?
questions.why: An adult has 206 bones.

questions.q: Which organ pumps blood?
questions.why: The heart pumps blood round the body.

questions.q: Where does most digestion start to happen after the mouth?
questions.why: Food moves from the mouth to the stomach.

questions.q: Match each system to its job.
questions.why: Each system has a job.

questions.q: What do muscles do to bones?
questions.why: Muscles can only pull.

questions.q: Why does your heart beat faster when you run?
o: Your body is hungry for more food to eat
Your skin gets hot and sweaty
questions.why: The heart pumps faster to deliver oxygen.

questions.q: Put in order: the path of food through the body.
questions.why: Food travels down the gut in this order.

questions.q: Which system protects the brain?
questions.why: The skull is a hard case around the brain.

questions.q: Explain why the biceps and triceps muscles come as a pair.
questions.model: Muscles can only pull, not push. One muscle pulls the arm to bend it, and the other pulls the arm to straighten it, so they work as an opposing pair.
questions.why: Opposing muscle pairs produce movement in both directions.

questions.q: A person breathes in. Which organs fill with air?
questions.why: Air goes to the lungs.

panel.q: Why is swallowing food not enough to give you energy?
o: It must be digested and absorbed into the blood
The heart then needs to chew it into small pieces
Bones must break it down first
Nothing more is needed once swallowed
panel.why: Digestion breaks food into small molecules that are absorbed.

panel.q: A broken leg bone also affects the muscles. Why?
o: Muscles are attached to the bone
Muscles are inside the bone marrow
panel.why: Muscles attach to bones through tendons, so a bone injury limits movement.

panel.q: Which sentence about the systems is best?
panel.why: Body systems depend on each other.

teach.topic: How body systems work together when you run
teach.model: When you run, your muscles pull on your bones to move you. Your lungs bring in oxygen, and your heart pumps blood to carry the oxygen to your muscles. Your brain controls it all.

points.ask: What moves you when you run?
How does oxygen get to the muscles?

stages.title: Plant anatomy
stages.hook: If you put a white flower in coloured water, its petals slowly change colour. How does the water get up there?
explain: A plant has roots, a stem, leaves and often flowers. Roots anchor the plant and take in water and minerals. The stem holds the leaves up and carries water and food through tubes. Leaves make food. Flowers make seeds.
Inside the stem are tiny tubes. Xylem tubes carry water up from the roots. Phloem tubes carry food made in the leaves to other parts.
In a flower, petals attract insects. The stamen makes pollen. The carpel contains ovules that can become seeds after pollination.

example.q: Celery in coloured water turns coloured. What carries the water?
steps: Water moves up the stem.
Tubes inside the stem carry it.
These tubes are called xylem.

analogies.home: Pipes in a house carry water. Xylem tubes carry water in plants.
analogies.farm: Farmers see crop roots drink water after rain.
analogies.nature: Tall trees lift water many metres to their highest leaves.

stages.mnemonic: Xylem = water up. Phloem = food all around.
terms: Anchors the plant and takes in water.
Tubes that carry water up the plant.
Tubes that carry sugars made in leaves.
Powder from the male part of a flower used to make seeds.

misc.wrong: Plants take their food from the soil.
misc.right: Plants make food in their leaves from light, water and carbon dioxide. Soil gives water and minerals.

trip.prompt: Find a labelled flower. Point out the petal, stamen and carpel.

questions.q: Which part of a plant takes in water from the soil?
questions.why: Roots take in water.

questions.q: Which tubes carry water up the stem?
questions.why: Xylem carries water up.

questions.q: What do petals do?
questions.why: Bright petals attract insects for pollination.

questions.q: Match the plant part to its job.
questions.why: Each part has a role.

questions.q: A farmer finds some plants wilting after a dry spell. Which part could not take in enough water?
questions.why: Roots absorb water, and wilting follows a lack of water.

questions.q: Put in order: water's journey in a plant.
questions.why: Water enters at the roots, rises through the stem and reaches the leaves.

questions.q: Which part of a flower makes pollen?
questions.why: The stamen makes pollen.

questions.q: A tree's bark is stripped in a ring around the trunk. Phloem is cut. What happens to the roots over time?
o: They starve because food cannot reach them
They grow faster because they get extra sunlight
They receive more water from the leaves
questions.why: Phloem carries food made in leaves down to the roots.

questions.q: Why do flowers often have bright petals and sweet nectar?
questions.model: Bright petals and nectar attract insects. The insects carry pollen from flower to flower, which helps the plant make seeds.
questions.why: Pollination by insects helps plants reproduce.

questions.q: Why are roots usually spread out and branched?
o: To anchor the plant and take in more water
To produce more seeds for next year
To catch more sunlight from above the soil
To attract bees and other insects
questions.why: More surface area absorbs more water and holds the plant firmly.

panel.q: Cut flowers last longer in water. Which explains this?
o: Xylem keeps supplying water to the petals
Roots grow quickly inside the vase
Leaves make food faster in water
Petals drink water directly from the vase
panel.why: Water continues to rise in the xylem of the stem.

panel.q: A plant is kept in the dark for a week. Which tubes would carry less food?
o: Phloem, because less food is made
Xylem, because it relies on light
Neither, because they carry only water
panel.why: Less light means less food is made in the leaves to be moved by phloem.

panel.q: A cactus has thick stems. What is likely?
panel.why: Thick stems store water for dry conditions.

teach.topic: How a plant takes water from the soil to its leaves
teach.model: Roots take in water from the soil. The water travels up through tiny tubes in the stem called xylem. It reaches the leaves, where it is used to make food.

points.ask: Where does it end up and why?

stages.title: Photosynthesis
stages.hook: A tree grows to be huge, but it never eats a meal. Where does all that new wood come from?
explain: Plants make their own food by photosynthesis. In the green parts, a pigment called chlorophyll captures light energy. The plant uses it to turn carbon dioxide and water into glucose (a sugar) and oxygen.
Word equation: carbon dioxide + water → glucose + oxygen, using light energy. Carbon dioxide enters through tiny holes in leaves called stomata. Water comes up from the roots.
The glucose is used for energy and growth, or stored as starch. The oxygen is released into the air, which animals use to breathe.

example.q: What are the two raw materials of photosynthesis?
steps: Plants take in gas from the air: carbon dioxide.
Plants take water from the soil.
These are the two inputs.

analogies.home: A kitchen turns ingredients into a meal, with heat as the energy. A leaf turns ingredients into sugar, with light as the energy.
analogies.farm: Crops need sun and rain to grow.
analogies.tech: A solar panel captures light energy, a leaf does too and stores it in sugar.

stages.mnemonic: Light, CO₂ and water in; sugar and oxygen out.
terms: Making food using light, water and carbon dioxide.
The green pigment that captures light.
A sugar made by plants for energy.
Tiny holes in leaves for gases.

misc.wrong: Plants breathe in oxygen only at night and carbon dioxide only in the day.
misc.right: Plants respire all day and night. In daylight they also photosynthesise, which makes more oxygen than they use.

trip.prompt: Find the equation and say which parts go in and which come out.

questions.q: What gas do plants take in for photosynthesis?
questions.why: Plants use carbon dioxide.

questions.q: Which gas is given out by photosynthesis?
questions.why: Oxygen is a product.

questions.q: What is chlorophyll?
o: A green pigment that captures light
A root hair that takes in water
A tiny seed that holds a new plant
A sugar stored in the stem and fruit
questions.why: Chlorophyll absorbs light energy.

questions.q: Put the steps of photosynthesis in order.
items: Light, CO₂ and water reach the leaf
Glucose is used or stored as starch
questions.why: The raw materials arrive first, chlorophyll captures the light energy, sugar is made, and then it is used or stored.

questions.q: Match each item to its role in photosynthesis.
questions.why: These are the key parts of the process.

questions.q: A plant is kept in a dark cupboard. What happens?
o: It cannot photosynthesise and becomes weak
It grows faster and taller than usual
It makes extra oxygen all through the night
It turns blue and then red
questions.why: Without light, the plant cannot make glucose.

questions.q: Pondweed in sunlight gives off bubbles. What are the bubbles likely to be?
questions.why: Photosynthesis releases oxygen.

questions.q: Where does most of the mass of a tree come from?
o: Mostly carbon from air carbon dioxide and water
Mostly minerals and salts that were taken from the soil
Mostly sunlight stored in the wood itself
Mostly oxygen gas taken in from the air
questions.why: Photosynthesis builds sugars from carbon dioxide and water, and these build wood.

questions.q: Why are most leaves broad, flat and thin?
questions.model: Flat, wide leaves have a large surface area to catch lots of light, and being thin means gases reach the cells quickly.
questions.why: Shape helps leaves capture light and exchange gases.

questions.q: A variegated leaf has green and white patches. After testing for starch, which part would show starch?
questions.why: Only green parts have chlorophyll for photosynthesis.

panel.q: Which is the best summary?
o: Plants convert light energy to chemical energy in sugar
Plants create new energy out of nothing at all
Plants feed by eating the soil around them
Plants burn up oxygen to make sugar in leaves
panel.why: Light energy is stored in glucose.

panel.q: Why does a forest help clean the air?
o: Leaves take in CO₂ and release oxygen
Leaves take in oxygen and release CO₂
Roots filter dust out of the air
Trees make smoke from their leaves
panel.why: Photosynthesis removes CO₂ and adds oxygen.

panel.q: Food chains start with plants. Why?
o: Plants make food using light energy
Plants are the biggest living things
Animals are unable to eat meat
panel.why: Plants are producers.

teach.topic: How a plant makes its own food
teach.model: Leaves use light energy to turn carbon dioxide and water into sugar. A green pigment called chlorophyll catches the light. Oxygen is released as a by-product.

points.ask: What energy does the plant use?

stages.title: Respiration
stages.hook: You breathe harder when you sprint. But is breathing the same as respiration?
explain: Breathing moves air in and out of the lungs. Respiration is a chemical process inside cells that releases energy from food, usually glucose. It happens in every living cell, all the time.
Aerobic respiration uses oxygen: glucose + oxygen → carbon dioxide + water + energy. We breathe out the carbon dioxide.
Plants respire too. They also photosynthesise in the light, so photosynthesis and respiration are like opposites, but both happen in plants.

example.q: Which gas goes into cells for respiration, and which comes out?
steps: Cells need oxygen to release energy from glucose.
Carbon dioxide is a waste product.
So oxygen goes in and carbon dioxide comes out.

analogies.home: A fire burns fuel to give heat. Cells slowly release energy from food in a gentle way.
analogies.sport: A runner who breathes hard is giving muscles more oxygen to release more energy.
analogies.tech: A battery stores energy and releases it, as glucose stores and releases energy in cells.

stages.mnemonic: Respiration = Release of energy. Breathing is just the delivery.
terms: Releasing energy from food in cells.
Moving air in and out of the lungs.

misc.wrong: Breathing and respiration mean the same thing.
misc.right: Breathing brings in oxygen. Respiration is the energy-releasing reaction in cells.

stages.limits: Muscles can also release energy without oxygen for a short time (anaerobic respiration), but it releases much less energy.

trip.prompt: Find the equation for aerobic respiration and compare it with photosynthesis.

questions.q: What is released during respiration?
questions.why: Respiration releases energy from food.

questions.q: Which gas is a waste product of aerobic respiration?
questions.why: Carbon dioxide is released.

questions.q: Where does respiration take place?
questions.why: Every living cell respires.

questions.q: Put in order: the journey of oxygen for respiration.
items: Oxygen goes into the blood in the lungs
Cells use it to release energy
questions.why: Oxygen is breathed in, carried by the blood and used in the cells.

questions.q: Match each word to its meaning.
pairs: Moving air into and out of lungs
questions.why: Each word names a different idea.

questions.q: After exercise, why do you keep breathing hard for a while?
o: Your body still needs oxygen to recover
Your lungs have gone to sleep for a while
Your skin is still cold from the air outside
questions.why: Muscles still need extra oxygen to return to normal.

questions.q: Mice in a sealed jar use up oxygen. What gas builds up?
questions.why: Respiration produces carbon dioxide.

questions.q: Does a plant respire? Explain your answer.
questions.model: Yes. Every living cell, including plant cells, releases energy from glucose by respiration, day and night.
questions.why: Respiration is a life process of all organisms.

questions.q: Why do athletes train to improve their heart and lungs?
o: To deliver oxygen to muscle cells faster
To make the muscle cells much smaller
To stop their cells respiring so quickly
To grow bigger and stronger lungs only
questions.why: More oxygen allows more aerobic respiration.

questions.q: A seed in wet soil gets warm. Why does its respiration speed up?
o: It stops growing in the warmth
It makes oxygen for the soil
It turns hard like a pebble
questions.why: Growing cells need energy.

panel.q: How are photosynthesis and respiration related?
o: One uses the products of the other
They are exactly the same process in reverse
Only animals carry out either one
panel.why: Photosynthesis makes glucose and oxygen; respiration uses them.

panel.q: Why does a sprinter breathe faster than someone standing still?
o: Muscles use more oxygen to release more energy
Air is much thinner on running tracks, so they gasp
Their heart stops for a little while
Their cells stop respiring at the start
panel.why: More activity means more respiration.

panel.q: If you hold your breath, what happens to the carbon dioxide in your body?
o: It builds up because you cannot breathe it out
It vanishes from the blood straight away and safely
It is turned into oxygen by the lungs
It is stored away inside the bones
panel.why: Cells keep respiring and making carbon dioxide.

teach.topic: The difference between breathing and respiration
teach.model: Breathing is moving air in and out of the lungs. Respiration happens inside cells. Cells use oxygen to release energy from glucose, and carbon dioxide is made as waste.

points.ask: What goes in and what comes out?

stages.title: Food chains and ecosystems
stages.hook: If all the grass vanished from a field, who would be in trouble besides the cows?
explain: An ecosystem is all the living things in an area and the non-living things they depend on, like water, soil and sunlight. Food chains show who eats whom and how energy passes along.

A food chain starts with a producer, a plant that makes food using sunlight. Next come consumers: herbivores eat plants, carnivores eat animals, omnivores eat both. Decomposers, such as fungi and bacteria, break down dead things and return nutrients to the soil.
The arrow in a food chain points in the direction the energy goes: from the thing eaten to the thing that eats it. Many chains join to form a food web.

example.q: In the chain grass → grasshopper → frog → snake, name the producer and a carnivore.
steps: Grass makes its own food: producer.
Frog eats grasshoppers: carnivore.
Snake eats frogs: carnivore.
example.a: Producer: grass. Carnivores: frog and snake.

analogies.farm: Grass feeds cows and people drink milk.
analogies.sea: Tiny plant-like plankton feed small fish, which feed larger fish.
analogies.nature: A fallen leaf is broken down by fungi to feed the soil.

stages.mnemonic: Arrows follow the energy: from eaten to eater.
terms: A living thing that makes its own food, like a plant.
A living thing that eats other living things.
A living thing that breaks down dead matter.

misc.wrong: In a food chain, the arrow points to the one being eaten.
misc.right: The arrow points from the food to the eater, showing the direction energy moves.

trip.prompt: Find a food web diagram. Trace one chain from a plant to a top predator.

questions.q: What is a producer?
o: A living thing that makes its own food
An animal that eats other animals for food
A dead leaf that has fallen on the ground
A hunter that chases its prey
questions.why: Plants are producers.

questions.q: Which animal is a herbivore?
questions.why: Rabbits eat plants.

questions.q: What do decomposers do?
questions.why: They recycle nutrients.

questions.q: Put in order: a food chain.
questions.why: Energy passes from producer to consumers.

questions.q: Match each organism to its role.
questions.why: Each plays a different role.

questions.q: In the chain grass → rabbit → fox, what does the arrow from grass to rabbit mean?
o: Energy goes from grass to the rabbit
The grass eats the rabbit when it is hungry
The rabbit makes the grass grow
The fox eats the grass first
questions.why: Arrows show the direction of energy transfer.

questions.q: In a pond, disease kills most of the small fish. What is likely to happen to the large fish that eat them?
o: They will have less food and may decrease
They will increase in number straight away
Their numbers will not be affected
questions.why: Less food limits predator numbers.

questions.q: Most food chains have only 4 or 5 links. What is the best reason?
o: Energy is lost at each step
Animals refuse to eat the last link
Plants stop growing at that point
There are not enough names to go round
questions.why: Much energy is lost as heat and waste at each link.

questions.q: Why are decomposers important to an ecosystem?
questions.model: Decomposers break down dead plants, animals and waste. This returns nutrients to the soil so that plants can use them again.
questions.why: They recycle nutrients.

questions.q: Which is a non-living part of an ecosystem?
questions.why: Sunlight, water and soil are non-living.

panel.q: Why are there fewer lions than zebras on a savanna?
o: Less energy is available at higher levels
Lions are lazier than zebras, so fewer survive
Zebras hunt and eat young lions
panel.why: Energy decreases along the chain, so fewer top predators can be supported.

panel.q: If an insecticide kills all the insects in a meadow, which effect is likely?
panel.why: Food chains link species, so removing one affects others.

panel.q: A fox eats both berries and mice. What is it?
panel.why: It eats both plants and animals.

teach.topic: How energy moves in a food chain
teach.model: Plants make food using sunlight. A herbivore eats the plant and gets energy. A carnivore eats the herbivore. The arrows show the energy moving along. Decomposers break down dead things.

stages.title: Reproduction and life cycles
stages.hook: A mother cat has kittens; a fern makes tiny dust-like spores; a strawberry plant sends out runners. All make new life. How are they different?
explain: Reproduction makes new organisms of the same kind. This keeps a species going. Different living things do it in different ways.

Many animals reproduce with eggs or live young. In plants, flowers make seeds after pollination. The seeds spread by wind, water or animals and grow when conditions are right. Some plants reproduce without seeds, such as potatoes growing from tubers or strawberries from runners.

A life cycle is the series of stages in an organism's life. A butterfly has four: egg, larva (caterpillar), pupa and adult. A frog: egg, tadpole, froglet and adult. Humans pass from baby to child, teenager and adult.

example.q: Name the stages of a butterfly's life cycle in order.
steps: Eggs are laid on a leaf.
A caterpillar hatches and grows.
It becomes a pupa.
An adult butterfly comes out.

analogies.farm: Hens lay eggs; a field of maize grows from seeds.
analogies.nature: A dandelion's seeds drift on the wind like tiny parachutes.
analogies.sea: A turtle lays eggs on the beach, and hatchlings crawl to the sea.

terms: The stages a living thing goes through.
Moving pollen to the part of a flower that makes seeds.
Spreading seeds away from the parent plant.
A big change of body form during growth.

misc.wrong: All plants grow only from seeds.
misc.right: Some plants also grow from bulbs, tubers, runners or cuttings.

trip.prompt: Pick a plant and an animal. Compare the stages in each life cycle.

questions.q: Put in order: a butterfly's life cycle.
questions.why: These stages are in this order.

questions.q: Put in order: a flowering plant's life cycle.
questions.why: A seed grows into an adult plant that makes new seeds.

questions.q: What is pollination?
o: Moving pollen to the carpel of a flower
Planting seeds in the soil each spring
Growing new roots underground in the dark
Making sugary nectar for visiting bees
questions.why: Pollen must reach the female part to make seeds.

questions.q: A dandelion seed has a fluffy top. How is it dispersed?
questions.why: The fluffy parachute catches the wind.

questions.q: Match the seed to how it spreads.
questions.why: Seeds have features that suit how they spread.

questions.q: A tadpole grows legs and loses its tail. Which stage is this?
questions.why: This is metamorphosis towards an adult frog.

questions.q: Why do seeds need to spread away from the parent plant?
o: To avoid competing for light and water
To grow bigger than their parent plant
To turn into animals later on
questions.why: Seedlings close to the parent would compete for resources.

questions.q: Why do flowers need bees or other pollinators?
questions.model: Bees carry pollen from one flower to another. Pollination is needed so the flower can make seeds and reproduce.
questions.why: Pollinators move pollen between flowers.

questions.q: A farmer grows potatoes by planting pieces of old potatoes. This is:
questions.why: New plants grow from tubers.

questions.q: A bird sits on eggs to keep them warm. Why?
o: To stop the chicks growing too fast
questions.why: Warmth is needed for development.

panel.q: Why do caterpillars and butterflies often eat different foods?
o: Their body forms are very different, so they avoid competing
The two forms dislike and fight each other, so they separate
Butterflies are unable to eat anything at all
Caterpillars are really a kind of plant
panel.why: Larvae feed on leaves while many adults drink nectar.

panel.q: What is the main benefit of seeds being spread by animals?
o: Animals get fat on the seeds
panel.why: Dispersal helps plants reach new habitats.

panel.q: A life cycle is described as a cycle. Why?
o: The adult makes new young, starting the stages again
It travels round in circles on the ground and never stops
It never ends for any single organism
It is shaped like a wheel with spokes
panel.why: Adults reproduce so the stages repeat in new individuals.

teach.topic: The life cycle of a flowering plant
teach.model: A seed grows into a seedling. The seedling becomes an adult plant with flowers. Pollination helps the flowers make new seeds. The seeds spread and grow, and the cycle repeats.

points.ask: What happens to the new seeds?

stages.title: Biodiversity and classification
stages.hook: There are millions of kinds of living things. How could you sort them so that scientists in every country agree?
explain: Biodiversity is the variety of life in a place or on Earth. Scientists sort living things into groups, which is called classification. Groups are based on shared features.

Animals are split into vertebrates (with a backbone) and invertebrates (without). Vertebrate groups are mammals, birds, reptiles, amphibians and fish. Invertebrates include insects, spiders and worms. Other big groups are plants, fungi and microorganisms.

Every species has a two-part Latin name, such as Homo sapiens for humans. A species is a group whose members can have fertile offspring together. Healthy ecosystems with lots of species are usually more stable.

example.q: A creature has a backbone, feathers and lays eggs. Which group?
steps: It has a backbone, so it is a vertebrate.
Feathers belong only to birds.
So it is a bird.

analogies.home: Sorting a library into fiction and non-fiction is like sorting life into groups.
analogies.city: A phone book groups people by street; scientists group living things by features.
analogies.nature: A rainforest has more species than a field of one crop.

stages.mnemonic: Mammals, Birds, Reptiles, Amphibians, Fish: MBRAF vertebrates.
terms: A group of the same kind of living thing that can breed together.

misc.wrong: A whale is a fish because it lives in water.
misc.right: A whale is a mammal. It breathes air, has hair at birth and feeds milk to its young.

stages.limits: Where to draw the lines between groups is sometimes debated, and DNA evidence has changed some classifications.

trip.prompt: Find a place in the world with very high biodiversity and name two living things there.

questions.q: What is biodiversity?
o: A type of healthy food from plants
questions.why: It means the variety of life.

questions.q: Which is an invertebrate?
questions.why: A spider has no backbone.

questions.q: What is the scientific name for humans?
questions.why: Humans are Homo sapiens.

questions.q: Match the animal to its group.
questions.why: Group is based on features.

questions.q: Order the groups from the broadest to the narrowest.
questions.why: Classification goes from big groups to small ones.

questions.q: A creature has six legs, three body parts and an exoskeleton. Which group?
questions.why: Six legs and three parts are insect features.

questions.q: A dolphin breathes air and feeds milk. Which group?
questions.why: Milk and air-breathing mean mammal.

questions.q: Why is a forest with many species usually more stable than a single-crop field?
o: If one species declines, others can fill its role
It has no changes in the weather at all, ever
It contains no animals that eat plants
Its plants never die or get eaten at all
questions.why: Variety gives resilience.

questions.q: Why do scientists use classification?
questions.model: Classification sorts living things into groups using shared features. It helps scientists identify, compare and study them and communicate clearly.
questions.why: It makes the huge variety of life manageable.

questions.q: A scientist finds a new insect. How would she name its species?
o: With one random number and a letter
questions.why: Species have a genus and species name.

panel.q: Why is protecting rainforests important for biodiversity?
o: They hold a very large number of species
They contain almost no insects or other small animals
They are very small in area
They contain only one tree type
panel.why: Many species live in rainforests, some found nowhere else.

panel.q: Which question would classify a pet cat as a mammal?
o: Does it have hair and feed milk to its young?
Does it sleep a lot each day and each night?
Is it cute and friendly to most people?
Does it purr when you stroke it?
panel.why: Hair and milk define mammals.

panel.q: A horse and a donkey can breed, but their offspring (mules) cannot usually reproduce. Why does this matter for the idea of species?
o: Species are defined by fertile offspring
Mules are a brand new species of horse
Horses are really a kind of insect or fish
Donkeys are really a kind of plant
panel.why: Members of the same species can have fertile offspring.

teach.model: Scientists sort animals using shared features. Animals with a backbone are vertebrates: mammals, birds, reptiles, amphibians and fish. Animals without a backbone, like insects, are invertebrates.

points.ask: What is the first big split?
How do you decide where an animal belongs?
